scientificEvidence.title: Effectiveness of interventions to promote help-seeking for mental health problems: systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Adults across 98 controlled studies with 69208 participants
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized controlled studies
scientificEvidence.finding: Interventions showed short-term improvements in several help-seeking outcomes and some longer-term formal help-seeking behavior. Effects varied by population and intervention type.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Few included studies came from low- and middle-income countries. No evidence was found for increased informal help seeking and general-public effects were not uniform.

scientificEvidence.title: School-based mental health literacy interventions to promote help-seeking: a systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Children and young people in 11 studies across 66 secondary schools
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.finding: The review found no strong evidence that school mental-health-literacy programs improved the measured help-seeking outcomes.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Measures and definitions were inconsistent and cost-effectiveness was not studied. This is youth and school evidence rather than direct evidence for the adult core-human track.

scientificEvidence.title: Interventions to improve mental health help-seeking attitudes intentions and behaviors: a systematic review of recent advances
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 54 randomized controlled trials published after 2016
scientificEvidence.method: Prospectively registered systematic review with narrative synthesis
scientificEvidence.finding: The review reports improvements across attitudes intentions or behaviors for several intervention families while emphasizing heterogeneity and weak standardization.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Outcome heterogeneity prevented a unified meta-analysis. Full author and study-level appraisal remain pending before claim use.

scientificEvidence.title: Do Web-based Mental Health Literacy Interventions Improve the Mental Health Literacy of Adult Consumers? Results From a Systematic Review
scientificEvidence.population: Adults in 14 web-intervention studies conducted mainly in high-income settings
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of randomized and quasi-experimental web interventions
scientificEvidence.finding: Structured tailored evidence-based and interactive web programs were more promising for literacy outcomes than unstructured information alone.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Most evidence came from Australia and the link from improved literacy to actual help seeking remained unclear. Transfer to Arabic-speaking Egyptian users is untested.

scientificEvidence.title: Mental health literacy measures evaluating knowledge attitudes and help-seeking: a scoping review
scientificEvidence.population: Quantitative mental-health-literacy measurement studies
scientificEvidence.method: Scoping review of measurement instruments and psychometrics
scientificEvidence.finding: The review identified many measures but far fewer validated instruments across knowledge stigma and help-seeking domains.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The search excluded non-English and grey literature and does not establish Arabic or Egyptian validity. Instrument licensing and updated validation require separate checks.

scientificEvidence.title: Situation analysis of gender and health in the Eastern Mediterranean Region
scientificEvidence.organization: WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean
authors: World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean
scientificEvidence.population: Populations of the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region with country examples including Egypt
scientificEvidence.method: Regional situation analysis synthesizing health-system and research evidence
scientificEvidence.finding: The report describes cultural acceptability stigma privacy concerns service factors and gendered beliefs as interacting barriers to mental-health help seeking in the region.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Regional synthesis cannot be treated as a single Egyptian population estimate. Each Egyptian example and cited study requires direct appraisal before curriculum use.

scientificEvidence.title: Relation between emotion regulation and mental health: a meta-analysis review
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 48 studies with a combined sample of 21150
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of associations between emotion-regulation strategies and mental-health indicators
scientificEvidence.finding: Emotion-regulation strategies were associated with mental-health indicators, and culture moderated some associations involving expressive suppression.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The synthesis is predominantly correlational, is not proof that teaching one strategy causes better mental health, and does not validate a one-size-fits-all hierarchy of strategies across cultures.

scientificEvidence.title: Effects of self-compassion interventions on reducing depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress: a meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 56 randomized controlled trials of self-compassion interventions
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.finding: The review found small-to-medium immediate effects and smaller follow-up effects for several distress outcomes.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Overall risk of bias was high, differences against active controls were often not significant, the review was not preregistered, and clinical intervention results cannot be assumed for a brief literacy exercise.

scientificEvidence.title: Examining domains of psychological flexibility and inflexibility as treatment mechanisms in acceptance and commitment therapy: A comprehensive systematic and meta-analytic review
scientificEvidence.population: Participants across 67 studies and 77 records with a combined sample of 9123 in ACT mechanism research
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analytic review of psychological flexibility and inflexibility as treatment mechanisms in acceptance and commitment therapy
scientificEvidence.finding: Changes in psychological flexibility and inflexibility were examined as mechanisms associated with outcomes in ACT research.
scientificEvidence.limitations: This is psychotherapy and mechanism evidence, not validation that a Motazen lesson is ACT or treatment. Samples, active comparisons, measurement choices, and clinical exclusions constrain transfer.

scientificEvidence.title: Targeting procrastination using psychological treatments: a systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 12 treatment studies with a combined sample of 718
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of psychological treatments targeting procrastination
scientificEvidence.finding: The pooled treatment effect was small and heterogeneous; a CBT subgroup appeared larger but contained only three studies.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous and concerned treatment studies. It does not justify promising that a brief productivity technique will resolve persistent procrastination.

scientificEvidence.title: Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 20 experimental health-behavior studies with a combined sample of 2601
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of self-reported habit strength or automaticity
scientificEvidence.finding: Habit formation time varied substantially by behavior and person rather than following a universal fixed-day rule.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Most included studies had high risk of bias, outcomes were self-reported, and the evidence concerns selected health behaviors rather than every daily-life habit.

scientificEvidence.title: The use and impact of self-monitoring on substance use outcomes: A descriptive systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Substance-use participants across 41 studies and 126 analyses
scientificEvidence.method: Descriptive systematic review of self-monitoring assessment effects
scientificEvidence.finding: Among moderate- or strong-quality analyses, self-monitoring was helpful in 29 percent, had no effect in 63 percent, and was detrimental in 8 percent.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The domain is substance use and cannot be generalized numerically to ordinary habit tracking. It is nevertheless direct counterevidence to claims that monitoring is universally beneficial or risk-free.

scientificEvidence.title: Do implementation intentions help to eat a healthy diet? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the empirical evidence
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in implementation-intention studies focused on dietary behavior
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.finding: Effects differed between increasing healthy foods and reducing unhealthy foods, and estimates varied with control and outcome quality.
scientificEvidence.limitations: This is older, domain-specific dietary evidence; it cannot establish equal effects for all goals or justify presenting if-then planning as sufficient by itself.

scientificEvidence.title: Sleep hygiene - What do we mean? A bibliographic review
scientificEvidence.population: Adult populations represented in 548 observational and intervention studies
scientificEvidence.method: Bibliographic review of definitions and components used in adult sleep-hygiene studies
scientificEvidence.finding: Only 44 percent of studies defined sleep hygiene, and included components and details varied substantially.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The review maps inconsistency rather than estimating the effectiveness of any specific behavior; it supports precise wording and component-level appraisal, not a generic sleep-hygiene prescription.

scientificEvidence.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: People with poor sleep or insomnia in 15 comparative studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis comparing sleep-hygiene education with CBT-I or mindfulness-based therapy
scientificEvidence.finding: Sleep-hygiene education was less effective than CBT-I, and only subjective measures showed significant improvement in the review.
scientificEvidence.limitations: No included study used sham or no-treatment comparison, and acceptability, adherence, understanding, and cost-effectiveness data were absent. Motazen must not present sleep education as insomnia treatment.

scientificEvidence.title: Interventions to improve social connections: a systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Adults in 58 controlled intervention studies with a mean age of 62 years
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.finding: Interventions affected objective social contact and perceived connection differently, with strategy-specific differences across those dimensions.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The mean participant age was 62 and intervention families were heterogeneous. Results do not imply that more contact always improves perceived connection or that a single exercise fits all adults.

scientificEvidence.title: Mindfulness-based programmes for mental health promotion in adults in nonclinical settings: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
scientificEvidence.population: 11605 adults in 136 randomized trials across 29 countries; 77 percent women
scientificEvidence.method: Preregistered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of expert-defined in-person programs
scientificEvidence.finding: Programs outperformed no intervention for several average outcomes, but did not show superiority to specific active controls and effects varied across settings.
scientificEvidence.limitations: GRADE confidence ranged from moderate to very low, many trials had high risk of bias, prediction intervals included no effect, and the studied multi-session teacher-led programs are not equivalent to a brief Motazen exercise.

scientificEvidence.title: Individual Resilience Interventions: A Systematic Review in Adult Population Samples over the Last Decade
scientificEvidence.organization: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
scientificEvidence.population: Adult samples across 38 controlled intervention articles
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA-guided systematic review of randomized and nonrandomized controlled studies
scientificEvidence.finding: Many studies reported statistically significant results, but definitions, methods, populations, and interventions varied greatly.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Samples often lacked power, methodological quality was fair, and heterogeneity prevented meaningful meta-analysis. Resilience must not be framed as a stable trait or an individual duty to tolerate harmful conditions.

scientificEvidence.title: The impact of psychological treatment on intolerance of uncertainty in generalized anxiety disorder: A systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 1199 adults with generalized anxiety disorder across 26 eligible studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of evidence-based psychological treatments
scientificEvidence.finding: Psychological treatments reduced intolerance of uncertainty and related symptoms in adults with generalized anxiety disorder.
scientificEvidence.limitations: This is clinical treatment evidence for diagnosed GAD, not proof that a general literacy lesson treats anxiety. Apparent superiority of directly targeted CBT was not maintained at follow-up.

scientificEvidence.title: Effectiveness of psychological treatments for depressive disorders in primary care: systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 5159 adults with depression in 30 primary-care trials
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis by therapy and delivery mode
scientificEvidence.finding: Psychological treatments overall showed benefit, while the estimate for face-to-face problem-solving therapy crossed no effect in this synthesis.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Clinical treatment evidence does not validate a general problem-solving worksheet as treatment. Therapy type, delivery, comparator, and population affect estimates.

scientificEvidence.title: Debiasing Health-Related Judgments and Decision Making: A Systematic Review
scientificEvidence.population: Lay people and health professionals in 87 studies reported across 68 articles
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of experimental and quasi-experimental debiasing interventions
scientificEvidence.finding: Most interventions were at least partially successful, but strategies, target biases, outcomes, and study quality varied.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Students dominated samples, many reports omitted power or measurement-quality information, and partial short-term task success does not establish durable transfer to consequential everyday decisions.

scientificEvidence.title: Mental health literacy and help-seeking behaviour among Egyptian undergraduates: a cross-sectional national study
scientificEvidence.population: 1740 undergraduates from ten Egyptian universities across four regions; 71.6 percent female
scientificEvidence.method: Online convenience-sample cross-sectional survey using mental-health-literacy and help-seeking questionnaires
scientificEvidence.finding: Mental-health-literacy dimensions related differently to help-seeking; professional help seeking was uncommon, personal relationships mattered, and urban-rural and demographic differences appeared.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Convenience sampling, self-report, cross-sectional design, online recruitment, female and medical-student overrepresentation, and a student-only population prevent causal or national-adult generalization.

scientificEvidence.title: Pattern, barriers, and predictors of mental health care utilization among Egyptian undergraduates: a cross-sectional multi-centre study
scientificEvidence.population: Egyptian undergraduates recruited across multiple universities
scientificEvidence.method: Cross-sectional survey using psychological-distress questions and the BACE-30 barriers measure
scientificEvidence.finding: Wanting to solve the problem alone was the leading reported barrier, alongside attitudinal, stigma-related, and instrumental barriers.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Self-report and cross-sectional student evidence cannot establish causality or represent all Egyptian adults; stated need, intentions, and actual service use must remain distinct.

scientificEvidence.title: Electronic Mental Health as an Option for Egyptian Psychiatry: Cross-Sectional Study
scientificEvidence.population: 188 Egyptian psychiatrists responding to an online survey sent to 640
scientificEvidence.method: Cross-sectional provider survey on system efficiency and electronic mental-health attitudes
scientificEvidence.finding: Responding psychiatrists generally supported electronic mental health as an adjunct and identified access and convenience opportunities while noting technology and therapeutic-rapport concerns.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Low response rate, unvalidated self-report survey, internet-user sampling bias, provider-only perspective, and 2020 technology conditions prevent treating enthusiasm as evidence of user benefit or current feasibility.

scientificEvidence.title: Understanding experiences of mental health help-seeking in Arab populations around the world: a systematic review and narrative synthesis
scientificEvidence.population: Arab adults represented in 74 included articles across Arab countries and diaspora settings
scientificEvidence.method: Prospectively registered systematic review with narrative synthesis
scientificEvidence.finding: Reported barriers included stigma, privacy and confidentiality, trust, literacy, language, logistics, and culture, while informal family and friend support was often preferred.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Most studies measured attitudes or intentions rather than actual use, Arab populations and settings are heterogeneous, and regional synthesis cannot be used as an Egyptian prevalence estimate.

scientificEvidence.title: Investigating the effects of marriage and relationship education on couples' communication skills: a meta-analytic study
scientificEvidence.population: Couples represented in 143 evaluations from 97 relationship-education reports
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of marriage and relationship education evaluations
scientificEvidence.finding: The synthesis found modest communication effects that differed by participant distress, follow-up, and measurement method.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Older couple-program evidence does not establish that a short generic script improves every relationship or transfers across culture, power imbalance, coercion, or violence.

scientificEvidence.title: The effectiveness of assertiveness communication training programs for healthcare professionals and students: A systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Healthcare professionals and students in eight included papers
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review with independent quality appraisal
scientificEvidence.finding: Training showed some benefits, while behavioral outcomes were mainly assessed in simulation and evidence for sustained behavior and safety outcomes remained limited.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Small occupational evidence base cannot validate a universal boundary script or assume that speaking up is equally safe across hierarchies, families, workplaces, and abusive contexts.

scientificEvidence.title: Do relationship education programs reduce relationship aggression? A meta-analytic study
scientificEvidence.population: 25527 participants across 31 relationship-education studies
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of control trials and pre-post studies
scientificEvidence.finding: The overall association with reduced aggression was small, and the randomized-trial estimate was not statistically significant while pre-post estimates were larger.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Combining designs complicates causal interpretation. Relationship education must not be presented as a safety response to active coercion or violence, which requires survivor-centered assessment and services.

scientificEvidence.title: Forgiveness Therapy for the Promotion of Mental Well-Being: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Adolescents and adults in randomized trials after varied interpersonal hurts or violence
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of process-based forgiveness interventions
scientificEvidence.finding: Structured process-based interventions showed average improvements in several wellbeing outcomes and forgiveness measures.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Therapy evidence does not create a duty to forgive, reconcile, contact, remain with, or confront a person who caused harm. Safety and autonomy take priority.

scientificEvidence.title: Impacts of digital social media detox for mental health: A systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in ten digital-detox studies published from 2013 through 2023
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis with risk-of-bias appraisal
scientificEvidence.finding: The synthesis found a small reduction in depressive symptoms but no statistically significant average effects for life satisfaction, stress, or overall wellbeing.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Only ten heterogeneous studies were included, detox definitions varied, and mental-health outcomes cannot be attributed to screen minutes alone.

scientificEvidence.title: Psychological Inoculation for Credibility Assessment, Sharing Intention, and Discernment of Misinformation: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 42530 participants across 42 independent studies
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA-guided systematic review and meta-analysis with moderator analyses
scientificEvidence.finding: Inoculation produced small improvements in credibility and sharing discernment, but did not significantly reduce misinformation sharing intention overall.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Task performance and intention are not durable real-world sharing behavior; English-language studies and intervention-specific findings require cultural and Arabic-language testing.

scientificEvidence.title: Inoculation and accuracy prompting increase accuracy discernment in combination but not alone
scientificEvidence.population: 7286 online participants across five studies
scientificEvidence.method: Five experiments using real-world true and false headlines with intervention combinations
scientificEvidence.finding: An emotional-manipulation inoculation alone did not improve truth discernment, while combining it with an accuracy prompt did.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Headline tasks do not prove long-term behavior change; several authors disclosed Google or Meta funding or employment, so replication and conflict-aware appraisal matter.

scientificEvidence.title: Interventions designed to improve financial capability: A systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 24 unique financial-capability studies conducted in OECD countries
scientificEvidence.method: Comprehensive systematic review of randomized and quasi-experimental interventions combining education with a product or service
scientificEvidence.finding: The review found insufficient comparable evidence to conclude that financial-capability interventions reliably improve financial behavior or outcomes.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Evidence was sparse, heterogeneous, and limited to OECD settings; personal education cannot overcome low income, inflation, debt terms, labor conditions, or missing consumer protections.

scientificEvidence.title: Organizational interventions and occupational burnout: a meta-analysis with focus on exhaustion
scientificEvidence.organization: International Archives of Occupational and Environmental Health
scientificEvidence.population: Active workers in 13 organizational or combined intervention studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis with GRADE appraisal
scientificEvidence.finding: Organizational and combined interventions produced a small average reduction in exhaustion.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Evidence quality was very low with heterogeneity, bias risk, and few studies. Individual coping advice must not displace workload, schedule, control, safety, or organizational responsibility.

scientificEvidence.title: A Meta-Analytic Review of Interventions That Promote Meaning in Life
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 33 randomized controlled trials of meaning-in-life interventions
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis by intervention and control type
scientificEvidence.finding: Meaning-in-life outcomes improved on average, with much larger estimates against passive than active controls and considerable heterogeneity.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Meaning is culturally and personally plural; heterogeneous effects do not justify prescribing one purpose, moral hierarchy, career path, or spiritual frame.

scientificEvidence.title: Exploring the Effects of Volunteering on the Social, Mental, and Physical Health and Well-being of Volunteers: An Umbrella Review
scientificEvidence.population: Participants represented in 28 reviews, mainly older adults in the United States
scientificEvidence.method: Prospectively registered umbrella review with AMSTAR 2 quality appraisal
scientificEvidence.finding: Reviews reported benefits across several domains, but review quality was generally poor and populations were concentrated among older US adults.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Selection, access, health status, role quality, unpaid-labor burden, and preexisting motivation complicate causal interpretation; volunteering must remain optional and non-exploitative.

scientificEvidence.title: The State of Web Accessibility for People with Cognitive Disabilities: A Rapid Evidence Assessment
scientificEvidence.population: People age nine and older living with cognitive impairment represented in 45 papers
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic rapid evidence assessment across three databases
scientificEvidence.finding: Persistent barriers remain despite standards, and meaningful solutions require attention to lived experience, tools, and inclusive research practice.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The evidence base is heterogeneous and cannot replace direct participation by Arabic-speaking Egyptian users with varied disabilities.

scientificEvidence.title: Retrieval Practice Consistently Benefits Student Learning: A Systematic Review of Applied Research in Schools and Classrooms
scientificEvidence.population: 5374 learners across 50 experiments in applied school and classroom settings
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review with 49 coded effect sizes from classroom research
scientificEvidence.finding: Retrieval practice improved later learning across varied classroom conditions, with 57 percent of effects reported as medium or large.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Only 6 percent of experiments were conducted in non-WEIRD countries; school and classroom test performance does not establish adult Egyptian behavior change or clinical benefit.

scientificEvidence.title: Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis
scientificEvidence.population: 10382 participants represented in 122 experiments and 192 transfer effect sizes
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analytic review of published and unpublished experiments across more than 40 years
scientificEvidence.finding: Practice testing produced a moderate average transfer benefit relative to re-exposure, but transfer varied strongly with task congruence, elaboration, and initial retrieval success.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Bias-adjusted intercepts were substantially smaller and sometimes indicated no positive transfer when favorable moderators were absent; knowledge transfer is not real-world behavior change.

scientificEvidence.title: The Distributed Practice Effect on Classroom Learning: A Meta-Analytic Review of Applied Research
scientificEvidence.population: More than 3000 learners represented in 22 reports and 31 classroom effect sizes
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of curriculum-relevant classroom studies
scientificEvidence.finding: Distributed practice showed a moderate average advantage over massed practice for classroom learning.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The small study pool prevented a comprehensive moderator analysis; classroom retention evidence does not determine one ideal spacing schedule for Motazen or prove behavioral transfer.

scientificEvidence.title: The efficacy of microlearning in improving self-care capability: a systematic review of the literature
scientificEvidence.population: People of varied ages represented in 26 controlled microlearning studies
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA-reported systematic review with Cochrane and ROBINS-I risk-of-bias appraisal
scientificEvidence.finding: Microlearning often improved cognitive self-care outcomes, while actual self-care behavior improved in only a minority of studies that measured it.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Twenty-five of 26 studies had moderate-to-high risk of bias; the evidence does not establish a universal lesson length, daily dose, or reliable behavior change.

scientificEvidence.title: Attrition and adherence in smartphone-delivered interventions for mental health problems: A systematic and meta-analytic review
scientificEvidence.organization: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 70 randomized controlled trials of smartphone-delivered mental-health interventions
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic and meta-analytic review of trial attrition and qualitative synthesis of adherence
scientificEvidence.finding: Average study attrition was substantial and intervention use commonly declined over time; no participant baseline characteristic reliably predicted attrition.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Clinical intervention trials are not equivalent to an educational curriculum, and reminders or compensation associated with retention do not justify manipulative engagement design.

scientificEvidence.title: Retention and Engagement in Culturally Adapted Digital Mental Health Interventions: Systematic Review of Dropout, Attrition, and Adherence in Non-WEIRD Settings
scientificEvidence.population: 4656 adults across 23 randomized trials of culturally adapted digital mental-health interventions in non-WEIRD settings
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA-guided systematic review of attrition, dropout, adherence, adaptation depth, and methodological quality
scientificEvidence.finding: Deeper participatory adaptation was associated with more favorable retention than surface translation alone in the included trials.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The evidence is associative across heterogeneous clinical interventions, not proof that adaptation causes retention or that the reported figures transfer to Egypt or Motazen.

scientificEvidence.title: Teach-back: A systematic review of implementation and impacts
scientificEvidence.population: Patients and clinicians represented in health-service teach-back studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of implementation strategies, fidelity, and knowledge or self-care impacts
scientificEvidence.finding: Teach-back can support knowledge and self-care in clinical communication, while implementation and fidelity reporting are inconsistent.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Motazen cannot conduct clinician-patient teach-back; it can only adapt the nonjudgmental comprehension-check principle and must test it directly in Arabic.

scientificEvidence.title: Putting Feelings Into Words: Affect Labeling as Implicit Emotion Regulation
scientificEvidence.population: Participants across laboratory, neuroimaging, and selected clinical affect-labeling studies
scientificEvidence.method: Narrative review comparing experiential, autonomic, neural, and behavioral affect-labeling evidence
scientificEvidence.finding: Putting emotions or evocative stimuli into words can alter some emotional-response indicators, but effects vary by task, timing, target, and whether labels are provided or self-generated.
scientificEvidence.limitations: This is not a systematic review; mechanisms remain speculative, self-generated labeling can initially increase affect, shame may respond differently, and Arabic language transfer is untested.

scientificEvidence.title: Emotion differentiation and behavioral dysregulation in clinical and nonclinical samples: A meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Clinical and nonclinical participants across 17 studies
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of negative emotion differentiation and maladaptive behaviors
scientificEvidence.finding: Greater negative-emotion differentiation was associated with slightly less maladaptive behavior on average, including after controlling for negative affect.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The association was small, studies were methodologically heterogeneous, and association does not prove that teaching labels changes behavior.

scientificEvidence.title: Shedding light on the association between repetitive negative thinking and deficits in cognitive control: A meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Clinical and nonclinical participants represented in 94 studies
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of repetitive negative thinking and multiple cognitive-control functions
scientificEvidence.finding: Repetitive negative thinking had a small association with difficulty discarding no-longer-relevant material from working memory, but not with the other tested control functions.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Primary studies and cognitive paradigms had reliability and sample-size limitations; the result rejects a broad claim that rumination reflects a global control deficit.

scientificEvidence.title: Health effects of psychological interventions for worry and rumination: A meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 36 randomized studies of nonpharmacological interventions targeting perseverative cognition
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of rumination, worry, physical, and behavioral outcomes
scientificEvidence.finding: Interventions reduced rumination and worry on average, while corresponding behavior and physical-health effects were smaller and professional delivery was associated with larger cognitive effects.
scientificEvidence.limitations: No intervention type clearly outperformed alternatives; treatment evidence must not be reframed as proof that a self-guided literacy lesson treats persistent rumination.

scientificEvidence.title: Effects of stress on decisions under uncertainty: A meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 1829 adult participants across 32 laboratory stress datasets
scientificEvidence.method: Random-effects meta-analysis of experimentally induced stress and decisions under uncertainty
scientificEvidence.finding: Laboratory stress produced a small average shift toward more disadvantageous, reward-seeking, or risky choices, with effects dependent on situation and stressor type.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The effect was small and laboratory tasks have limited ecological validity; stress does not make every person or decision uniformly irrational.

scientificEvidence.title: The effects of sleep deprivation on risky decision making
scientificEvidence.population: Healthy adults in experimental sleep-deprivation and risky-choice studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of risky decision-making effects and moderators
scientificEvidence.finding: Sleep deprivation had complex, inconsistent effects on risky decisions that varied with framing, task, duration, timing, sex, and other conditions.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The evidence does not support a deterministic claim that one poor night always causes riskier choices, and laboratory tasks may not represent daily decisions.

scientificEvidence.title: 20th Anniversary Update of the Ottawa Decision Support Framework Part 1: A Systematic Review of the Decisional Needs of People Making Health or Social Decisions
scientificEvidence.population: Decision makers, families, and practitioners across 45 health and social decision studies in seven countries
scientificEvidence.method: Mixed-studies systematic review with independent screening, quality appraisal, and narrative synthesis
scientificEvidence.finding: Decision needs include knowledge, values, support, roles, timing, expectations, information overload, powerful emotions, and family or practitioner involvement.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The framework centers health and social decisions and cannot be copied into every everyday choice; only peer-reviewed ODSF-based studies were included.

scientificEvidence.title: Can There Ever Be Too Many Options? A Meta-Analytic Review of Choice Overload
scientificEvidence.population: 5036 participants across 63 conditions from 50 published and unpublished choice experiments
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analytic review of motivation, choice, and satisfaction under larger versus smaller option sets
scientificEvidence.finding: The mean choice-overload effect was approximately zero with substantial between-study variation and no sufficient universal condition identified.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Consumer-choice experiments do not cover all high-stakes or personal decisions; contextual moderators may still produce overload in some settings.

scientificEvidence.title: The effect of caffeine on subsequent sleep: A systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Participants across 24 experimental caffeine and nighttime-sleep studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of caffeine dose, timing, and objective or subjective sleep outcomes
scientificEvidence.finding: Caffeine reduced total sleep and sleep efficiency on average, with dose- and timing-relevant effects.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Average timing estimates depend on dose, beverage, metabolism, medication, pregnancy, age, tolerance, and bedtime; they are not a universal curfew or medical instruction.

scientificEvidence.title: The association of screen time and the risk of sleep outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 548338 participants across 21 cohort studies and diverse age groups
scientificEvidence.method: Preregistered systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of screen time and sleep outcomes
scientificEvidence.finding: Longer screen time was associated with shorter sleep, later bedtime, and more sleep difficulties on average.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Cohort associations do not prove that screen exposure alone caused sleep outcomes; activity type, timing, displacement, content, work, and reverse causation matter.

scientificEvidence.title: A meta-analysis of techniques to promote motivation for health behaviour change from a self-determination theory perspective
scientificEvidence.population: Children and adults across 74 controlled health-behavior intervention studies; 80 percent were randomized or cluster-randomized
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of need-supportive techniques and self-determination mediators
scientificEvidence.finding: Need-supportive interventions improved perceived autonomy support, autonomy, competence, relatedness, and motivation on average, while individual techniques had limited independent impact and appeared to work in combinations.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The review concerns intervention mediators rather than a universal recipe for action, combines ages and behaviors, and does not validate a self-guided Egyptian curriculum.

scientificEvidence.title: Self-determination theory interventions for health behavior change: Meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.organization: Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in randomized controlled health-behavior interventions based on self-determination theory
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis and meta-analytic structural equation modeling of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.finding: Self-determination interventions produced a small average improvement in health behavior, with autonomous motivation and perceived competence among the tested mediating pathways.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The average behavioral effect was small; health-behavior trials do not show that motivation must precede every action or that one technique works for everyone.

scientificEvidence.title: Does the Mere Presence of a Smartphone Impact Cognitive Performance? A Meta-Analysis of the Brain Drain Effect
scientificEvidence.population: 7093 participants across 56 effects from smartphone-presence studies
scientificEvidence.method: Preregistered systematic review and six meta-analyses by cognitive outcome
scientificEvidence.finding: Only working-memory capacity showed a significant pooled negative effect; other cognitive outcomes were null, and methodological heterogeneity and low power limited inference.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Laboratory mere-presence manipulations do not cover active notifications, compulsive checking, content, or every real-world work context.

scientificEvidence.title: Digital self-control interventions for distracting media multitasking: A systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Users and learners in studies of software-based digital self-control interventions
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of intervention mechanisms, behavior, cognitive control, and performance outcomes
scientificEvidence.finding: Intervention mechanisms and effects varied; usage visualization alone was often ineffective, blocking strictness mattered, and the evidence did not establish digital self-control tools as a categorical solution.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Evidence was sparse, frequently student-centered, and heterogeneous; tools may create burden, work conflicts, avoidance, or compensatory use.

scientificEvidence.title: Social comparison and envy on social media: A critical review
scientificEvidence.population: Social-media users represented in prior reviews and studies published through 2021
scientificEvidence.method: Critical synthesis of prior reviews and recent evidence on comparison, envy, and wellbeing
scientificEvidence.finding: Earlier studies commonly linked online comparison and envy to poorer wellbeing, while newer findings include positive, heterogeneous, conditional, reciprocal, and person-specific effects.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Much evidence is observational, platform-specific, self-reported, and vulnerable to reverse causation; it does not prove that passive use harms every person.

scientificEvidence.title: Social media use and well-being: What we know and what we need to know
scientificEvidence.population: Social-media users across hundreds of studies included in 27 reviews published from 2019 through August 2021
scientificEvidence.method: Umbrella review of nine meta-analyses, nine systematic reviews, and nine narrative reviews
scientificEvidence.finding: Reviews drawing from overlapping evidence reached disagreeing conclusions, especially for time spent and active versus passive use, emphasizing person-specific and methodological variation.
scientificEvidence.limitations: An umbrella synthesis inherits weaknesses of its reviews and cannot identify an individual user's cause or optimal usage rule.

scientificEvidence.title: Anger and emotion regulation strategies: a meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Clinical and nonclinical participants across 81 studies and 115 effect sizes
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis of associations between anger and avoidance, acceptance, distraction, reappraisal, rumination, and suppression
scientificEvidence.finding: Anger was positively associated with avoidance, rumination, and suppression and negatively associated with acceptance and reappraisal, but heterogeneity was large across every analysis.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Associations do not establish that teaching one strategy will prevent aggression; effects varied by anger type, clinical and criminal status, culture, study quality, and sample composition.

scientificEvidence.title: A meta-analytic review of anger management activities that increase or decrease arousal: What fuels or douses rage?
scientificEvidence.population: 10189 participants across 154 studies and 184 independent samples
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analytic review comparing arousal-decreasing and arousal-increasing anger-management activities
scientificEvidence.finding: Arousal-decreasing activities reduced anger and aggression on average, whereas arousal-increasing activities were ineffective overall and did not support venting as an anger-reduction strategy.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The synthesis combines distinct activities, populations, delivery modes, and outcomes; it does not make every breathing or meditation exercise universally safe or replace violence-risk assessment.

scientificEvidence.title: Egypt STEPS Survey 2017 Fact Sheet
scientificEvidence.organization: World Health Organization, Egypt Ministry of Health and Population, and CAPMAS
authors: Egypt Ministry of Health and Population
Central Agency for Public Mobilization and Statistics
scientificEvidence.population: 6680 Egyptian adults aged 15 to 69 with a 94.3 percent response rate
scientificEvidence.method: Population-based stratified cluster random survey with behavioral, physical, and biochemical STEPS measures
scientificEvidence.finding: The national survey documented substantial variation by sex and behavior, including 24.9 percent with insufficient physical activity and large sex differences in vigorous activity and tobacco use.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The 2017 snapshot is historical, covers NCD risk rather than Motazen outcomes, relies partly on self-report, and cannot prescribe individual behavior or explain structural constraints.

scientificEvidence.title: Mental health literacy: a comparative study on stigmatizing attitude and help-seeking behavior towards mental disorders between adolescents and adults
scientificEvidence.organization: Journal of the Egyptian Public Health Association
scientificEvidence.population: 369 adolescents and adults attending Ain Shams University Hospitals outpatient clinics in 2022 to 2023
scientificEvidence.method: Arabic questionnaire using validated knowledge, attitude, and reported or intended behavior scales
scientificEvidence.finding: Knowledge, attitudes, and reported or intended behavior differed between adults and adolescents and varied by education, urban residence, employment, sex, and familiarity with mental illness.
scientificEvidence.limitations: A hospital-outpatient convenience context and mixed age sample cannot represent all Egyptian adults or establish that literacy changes actual service use.

scientificEvidence.title: National Survey of Prevalence of Mental Disorders in Egypt: preliminary survey
scientificEvidence.population: 14640 adults aged 18 to 64 in households across five Egyptian regions
scientificEvidence.method: Door-to-door multiregion household survey using the MINI-Plus diagnostic interview
scientificEvidence.finding: The preliminary survey found meaningful adult mental-health burden and associations with sociodemographic and physical-health factors across the studied regions.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Fieldwork and diagnostic frameworks are old, only five regions were covered, and the estimate must not be presented as current prevalence or converted into a Motazen user diagnosis.

scientificEvidence.title: Adverse events in meditation practices and meditation-based therapies: a systematic review
scientificEvidence.population: Adults across experimental, observational, and case reports of meditation practices or therapies
scientificEvidence.method: Broad-sweep systematic review of somatic, psychiatric, neurological, and cognitive adverse events
scientificEvidence.finding: Adverse experiences were reported across study types, including anxiety, depression, cognitive anomalies, fear, dissociation, trauma re-experience, and rare severe events; estimates varied greatly by study design.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Retrospective reports, case studies, retreat exposure, inconsistent definitions, selection, attribution, and sparse longitudinal data prevent a precise Motazen risk estimate.

scientificEvidence.title: The empirical status of mindfulness-based interventions: A systematic review of 44 meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials
scientificEvidence.population: Participants across 44 meta-analyses of randomized mindfulness-based intervention trials
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of randomized-trial meta-analyses covering effects, heterogeneity, bias, moderators, and harms reporting
scientificEvidence.finding: Benefits varied by population, comparator, and outcome, while adverse-event reporting was inconsistent and often absent from the underlying evidence.
scientificEvidence.limitations: A review of reviews inherits overlap, reporting gaps, and heterogeneity and does not establish the safety or efficacy of an unguided micro-practice for a particular user.

scientificEvidence.title: Posttraumatic growth and recovery among a sample of Egyptian mental health service users: a phenomenological study
scientificEvidence.population: 17 community-dwelling Egyptian adults from three governorates who identified as recovered or recovering from mental-health issues
scientificEvidence.method: Semi-structured interviews with inductive thematic analysis
scientificEvidence.finding: Participants described recovery in personal and functional terms including relationships, spirituality, new possibilities, identity and strengths, appreciation of life, acceptance, forgiveness, hope, and clinical recovery.
scientificEvidence.limitations: A small purposive service-user sample cannot define recovery for all Egyptians, prove posttraumatic growth, or justify pressuring people to find benefit in trauma.

scientificEvidence.title: Role of traditional healers in the pathway of service for a sample of obsessive compulsive disorder patients in Egypt
scientificEvidence.population: 93 Egyptian patients with clinician-confirmed obsessive-compulsive disorder at a specialist setting
scientificEvidence.method: Clinical diagnostic confirmation and study-specific questionnaire on help-seeking pathway
scientificEvidence.finding: In this narrow clinical sample, traditional-healer use often preceded psychiatric advice and was associated with stigma, religious interpretations, accessibility, trust, and social acceptance.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The small specialist OCD sample and study-specific questionnaire cannot represent religion, traditional care, or help-seeking among all Egyptians; reported beliefs are not causal proof.

scientificEvidence.title: Identity Development and Well-being: A Systematic Review
scientificEvidence.organization: Studia Doctoralia Psychology and Educational Science
scientificEvidence.population: Participants in 10 identity-development and wellbeing studies published from 1990 through 2024
scientificEvidence.method: PRISMA systematic review across five databases and reference lists
scientificEvidence.finding: Identity commitment related to identity development, but findings for in-depth exploration were inconsistent and the identity-wellbeing relationship remained unclear.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Only 10 studies met criteria, cultural and age transfer are uncertain, and the evidence does not validate an identity-building exercise or a fixed ideal self.

scientificEvidence.title: Adult friendship and wellbeing: A systematic review with practical implications
scientificEvidence.population: Adults aged 18 to 65 across 38 studies, predominantly young adults and university students
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review of adult friendship variables and multidimensional wellbeing
scientificEvidence.finding: Friendship quality, socializing, supportive reactions, autonomy support, and maintenance efforts were commonly associated with wellbeing, while evidence was often sparse, contradictory, or population-specific.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Most evidence was cross-sectional and student-heavy, friend dyads and longitudinal studies were rare, and association does not justify pressure to make or keep unsafe friendships.

scientificEvidence.title: Does time management work? A meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 53957 participants across 158 nonclinical quantitative studies
scientificEvidence.method: Broad meta-analysis of time-management measures, experiments, performance, wellbeing, and contextual correlates
scientificEvidence.finding: Time management had moderate associations with wellbeing and performance and a somewhat stronger relationship with wellbeing, but most studies were cross-sectional and interventions were poorly specified.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Causality is limited, heterogeneity is high, and access to controllable time depends on income, education, care work, job autonomy, and privilege.

scientificEvidence.title: Examining the relationship between civic engagement and mental health in young adults: a systematic review of the literature
scientificEvidence.population: Young adults across 53 civic-engagement and wellbeing studies
scientificEvidence.method: Systematic review and narrative synthesis across civic activity types, duration, directionality, mediators, and moderators
scientificEvidence.finding: Civic engagement had heterogeneous positive, negative, and null relationships with wellbeing depending on activity, duration, directionality, adversity, and participant context.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Young-adult evidence does not establish causal benefit, safety, political neutrality, or feasibility in Egypt and cannot justify compulsory participation.

scientificEvidence.title: Are Ethics Training Programs Improving? A Meta-Analytic Review of Past and Present Ethics Instruction in the Sciences
scientificEvidence.population: 10069 participants across 66 empirical studies, 106 science-ethics courses, and 150 effect sizes
scientificEvidence.method: Random-effects meta-analytic review including published and unpublished ethics-training evaluations
scientificEvidence.finding: Ethics instruction showed moderate average benefits, with stronger effects for knowledge, self-perception, and ethical decision making and important variation by field, criterion, practice, and course design.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Science and professional ethics courses cannot define a universal personal morality, prove real-world ethical behavior, or transfer directly to Egyptian civic and family dilemmas.

scientificEvidence.title: Self-esteem Interventions in Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: Adults across 119 intervention studies
scientificEvidence.method: Random-effects systematic review and meta-analysis of interventions targeting adult global self-esteem
scientificEvidence.finding: Interventions had a small-to-moderate average effect on measured global self-esteem, with substantial variation by intervention, format, contact, population, and comparator.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Heterogeneity, confounding between moderators, limited power, publication bias, and emphasis on the target measure prevent equating higher self-esteem scores with self-respect or broad wellbeing.

scientificEvidence.title: Effectively Communicating About HIV and Other Health Disparities: Findings From a Literature Review and Future Directions
scientificEvidence.population: Health-disparity communication research, with an emphasis on HIV-related disparities in the United States
scientificEvidence.method: Literature review and conceptual synthesis of message frames and unintended effects
scientificEvidence.finding: Individual-responsibility and social-comparison frames can create unintended blame, stigma, guilt, shame, or incomplete causal understanding; no single evidence-based framing solution was established.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The evidence base was limited, mostly disease- and US-specific, and does not directly test general life-responsibility lessons or Egyptian wording.

scientificEvidence.title: Effectiveness of Error Management Training: A Meta-analysis
scientificEvidence.population: 2183 participants across 24 identified training studies
scientificEvidence.method: Meta-analysis comparing error-management, error-avoidant, and exploratory training conditions
scientificEvidence.finding: Error-management training showed a positive average training effect with larger estimates for transfer and novel tasks; active exploration and explicit error encouragement were candidate effective elements.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Controlled skill-training errors are not equivalent to bereavement, trauma, injustice, moral injury, irreversible loss, or high-stakes real-world failure.

scientificEvidence.title: Do Growth Mindset Interventions Impact Students' Academic Achievement? A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis With Recommendations for Best Practices
scientificEvidence.population: 97672 students across 63 studies; smaller subsets met manipulation and higher-quality criteria
scientificEvidence.method: Best-practice appraisal and three meta-analyses with publication-bias and study-quality checks
scientificEvidence.finding: The overall achievement effect was very small and became nonsignificant after publication-bias correction; higher-quality and successful-manipulation subsets were nonsignificant.
scientificEvidence.limitations: The review concerns student achievement, not all forms of learning, recovery, accountability, or adult adaptation after setbacks.

scientificEvidence.title: Burden of Care, Depression, and Anxiety Among Family Caregivers of People With Dementia
scientificEvidence.organization: Journal of Primary Care and Community Health
scientificEvidence.population: 141 family caregivers attending a Cairo University psychiatric-hospital geriatric clinic, predominantly women and daughters
scientificEvidence.method: Cross-sectional questionnaire study using caregiver burden, anxiety, depression, and demographic measures
scientificEvidence.finding: Substantial caregiver burden and symptoms of anxiety and depression co-occurred in this clinical sample, with women and daughters forming most participants.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Single-site cross-sectional associations cannot represent all Egyptian families, establish causality, or define acceptable obligations and boundaries.

scientificEvidence.title: Psychosocial Family Interventions for Relatives of People Living With Psychotic Disorders in the Arab World: Systematic Review
scientificEvidence.population: Six family-intervention studies from Arab-region clinical settings
scientificEvidence.method: Five-database systematic review and narrative synthesis of culturally adapted family interventions
scientificEvidence.finding: The small evidence base suggested culturally adapted family intervention was feasible and acceptable, but included-study quality was generally poor and the domain was narrowly clinical.
scientificEvidence.limitations: Only six studies, clinical psychosis focus, generally poor methodological quality, and regional aggregation prevent transfer to everyday Egyptian family guidance.

professionalGuidelines.title: Psychological self-help interventions
professionalGuidelines.population: People who may benefit from structured psychological self-help within stepped care
professionalGuidelines.method: WHO implementation and intervention guidance page
professionalGuidelines.finding: WHO presents structured guided and unguided psychological self-help as a scalable component of care and links implementation manuals including Doing What Matters in Times of Stress.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: This guidance concerns psychological interventions and service delivery. Motazen is a literacy and capability product and must not imply that its curriculum is equivalent to a WHO intervention or treatment.

professionalGuidelines.title: Mental health and psychosocial support platform: mental health professionals
professionalGuidelines.organization: WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean
authors: World Health Organization Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean
professionalGuidelines.population: People seeking mental-health and psychosocial support in countries of the Eastern Mediterranean Region
professionalGuidelines.method: WHO regional directory page listing country support services
professionalGuidelines.finding: The page lists Egyptian national and professional mental-health support telephone routes with stated operating patterns.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: Directory entries may change and some originated during the COVID-19 response. Every number and operating time requires direct freshness confirmation before display; this source alone is not enough for emergency publishing.

professionalGuidelines.title: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
professionalGuidelines.population: Children adolescents adults older adults and specified populations including people with chronic conditions or disability
professionalGuidelines.finding: The guideline provides population-specific recommendations and emphasizes that some activity is better than none and that activity should be adapted to ability and health status.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: Motazen is not a medical assessment service. Recommendations must preserve subgroup qualifications, accessibility, gradual progression, and advice to seek appropriate professional guidance when needed.

professionalGuidelines.title: From loneliness to social connection: charting a path to healthier societies
authors: World Health Organization Commission on Social Connection
professionalGuidelines.population: Global populations across the life course
professionalGuidelines.method: WHO commission report synthesizing evidence and policy considerations
professionalGuidelines.finding: The report distinguishes loneliness, social isolation, and social connection and frames connection as shaped by individual, community, and structural conditions.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: A global policy synthesis does not predict an individual outcome and must not turn social difficulty into personal blame or imply that simply increasing contact resolves loneliness.

professionalGuidelines.title: Health care for women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence: a clinical handbook
professionalGuidelines.population: Women subjected to intimate partner violence or sexual violence; guidance intended for health-care providers
professionalGuidelines.method: WHO clinical handbook based on violence-response guidelines
professionalGuidelines.finding: First-line response prioritizes listening, needs, validation, safety, and ongoing support rather than generic conflict resolution.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: Motazen is not a clinical or emergency service and cannot conduct a private trained assessment. Local referral routes, device safety, and resource freshness require specialist verification.

professionalGuidelines.title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: guidance on large multi-modal models
professionalGuidelines.population: Developers, deployers, regulators, health providers, patients, and publics affected by generative AI for health
professionalGuidelines.method: WHO ethics and governance guidance with more than 40 recommendations
professionalGuidelines.finding: Health-related generative AI requires defined purposes, transparency, stakeholder participation, independent evaluation, privacy protection, accountability, and attention to inaccurate or biased outputs.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: Governance guidance does not validate any specific chatbot, model, or use case and does not prove benefit, safety, or suitability for Arabic-speaking Egyptian users.

professionalGuidelines.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
professionalGuidelines.population: People with visual, auditory, physical, speech, cognitive, language, learning, and neurological disabilities
professionalGuidelines.method: W3C Recommendation defining testable web accessibility success criteria
professionalGuidelines.finding: WCAG 2.2 provides a testable baseline for perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust web content.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: Conformance is necessary but not sufficient for usability, cognitive accessibility, Arabic quality, trauma sensitivity, or success with actual Motazen users.

professionalGuidelines.title: Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities
authors: W3C Cognitive and Learning Disabilities Accessibility Task Force
professionalGuidelines.population: People with cognitive and learning disabilities and neurodivergent users
professionalGuidelines.method: W3C Working Group Note containing user needs, objectives, patterns, personas, and co-design guidance
professionalGuidelines.finding: Usable content benefits from clear words, short sentences and blocks, separated instructions, predictable interaction, error prevention and recovery, adaptation, and participation by disabled users.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: This is supplemental guidance rather than a conformance standard; patterns require testing in Arabic, right-to-left layouts, low-energy states, and the actual product.

professionalGuidelines.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
professionalGuidelines.organization: American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
professionalGuidelines.method: Expert consensus using evidence review, RAND Appropriateness Method, discussion, and voting
professionalGuidelines.finding: The panel recommended regularly obtaining at least seven hours of sleep for adults aged 18 to 60 to support optimal health.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: This is a population recommendation, not an individual diagnosis or rigid target; sleep need varies and the statement does not resolve timing, regularity, quality, shift work, illness, or all consequences of long sleep.

professionalGuidelines.title: Sleep Deprivation and Deficiency: Healthy Sleep Habits
professionalGuidelines.organization: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute
authors: National Heart Lung and Blood Institute
professionalGuidelines.population: General public including adults and shift workers
professionalGuidelines.method: Government health education guidance on schedule, light, caffeine, environment, naps, activity, and shift work
professionalGuidelines.finding: The guidance recommends protecting sleep opportunity and testing practical schedule, light, stimulant, environment, and activity changes while recognizing shift-work constraints.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: General guidance does not diagnose or treat a sleep disorder and must be adapted for caregiving, housing, work schedules, disability, medication, pain, and local living conditions.

professionalGuidelines.title: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: diagnosis and management (NG87)
professionalGuidelines.organization: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
professionalGuidelines.population: Children, young people, and adults with possible or diagnosed ADHD
professionalGuidelines.method: Evidence-based clinical guideline with explicit adult referral and specialist diagnostic recommendations; last reviewed May 2025
professionalGuidelines.finding: For adults without a childhood diagnosis, referral is indicated when typical manifestations began in childhood, persisted, are not better explained, and cause at least moderate impairment; diagnosis requires trained specialist assessment across history and settings and cannot rest on a rating scale alone.
professionalGuidelines.limitations: This UK guideline does not define Egyptian referral pathways or diagnose any Motazen user; local clinical review and service mapping remain required.

systematicReviews.title: Effectiveness of interventions to promote help-seeking for mental health problems: systematic review and meta-analysis
systematicReviews.population: Adults across 98 controlled studies with 69208 participants
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized and non-randomized controlled studies
systematicReviews.finding: Interventions showed short-term improvements in several help-seeking outcomes and some longer-term formal help-seeking behavior. Effects varied by population and intervention type.
systematicReviews.limitations: Few included studies came from low- and middle-income countries. No evidence was found for increased informal help seeking and general-public effects were not uniform.

systematicReviews.title: School-based mental health literacy interventions to promote help-seeking: a systematic review
systematicReviews.population: Children and young people in 11 studies across 66 secondary schools
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review of randomized controlled trials
systematicReviews.finding: The review found no strong evidence that school mental-health-literacy programs improved the measured help-seeking outcomes.
systematicReviews.limitations: Measures and definitions were inconsistent and cost-effectiveness was not studied. This is youth and school evidence rather than direct evidence for the adult core-human track.

systematicReviews.title: Interventions to improve mental health help-seeking attitudes intentions and behaviors: a systematic review of recent advances
systematicReviews.population: Participants in 54 randomized controlled trials published after 2016
systematicReviews.method: Prospectively registered systematic review with narrative synthesis
systematicReviews.finding: The review reports improvements across attitudes intentions or behaviors for several intervention families while emphasizing heterogeneity and weak standardization.
systematicReviews.limitations: Outcome heterogeneity prevented a unified meta-analysis. Full author and study-level appraisal remain pending before claim use.

systematicReviews.title: Do Web-based Mental Health Literacy Interventions Improve the Mental Health Literacy of Adult Consumers? Results From a Systematic Review
systematicReviews.population: Adults in 14 web-intervention studies conducted mainly in high-income settings
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review of randomized and quasi-experimental web interventions
systematicReviews.finding: Structured tailored evidence-based and interactive web programs were more promising for literacy outcomes than unstructured information alone.
systematicReviews.limitations: Most evidence came from Australia and the link from improved literacy to actual help seeking remained unclear. Transfer to Arabic-speaking Egyptian users is untested.

systematicReviews.title: Mental health literacy measures evaluating knowledge attitudes and help-seeking: a scoping review
systematicReviews.population: Quantitative mental-health-literacy measurement studies
systematicReviews.method: Scoping review of measurement instruments and psychometrics
systematicReviews.finding: The review identified many measures but far fewer validated instruments across knowledge stigma and help-seeking domains.
systematicReviews.limitations: The search excluded non-English and grey literature and does not establish Arabic or Egyptian validity. Instrument licensing and updated validation require separate checks.

systematicReviews.title: Relation between emotion regulation and mental health: a meta-analysis review
systematicReviews.population: Participants in 48 studies with a combined sample of 21150
systematicReviews.method: Meta-analysis of associations between emotion-regulation strategies and mental-health indicators
systematicReviews.finding: Emotion-regulation strategies were associated with mental-health indicators, and culture moderated some associations involving expressive suppression.
systematicReviews.limitations: The synthesis is predominantly correlational, is not proof that teaching one strategy causes better mental health, and does not validate a one-size-fits-all hierarchy of strategies across cultures.

systematicReviews.title: Effects of self-compassion interventions on reducing depressive symptoms, anxiety, and stress: a meta-analysis
systematicReviews.population: Participants in 56 randomized controlled trials of self-compassion interventions
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
systematicReviews.finding: The review found small-to-medium immediate effects and smaller follow-up effects for several distress outcomes.
systematicReviews.limitations: Overall risk of bias was high, differences against active controls were often not significant, the review was not preregistered, and clinical intervention results cannot be assumed for a brief literacy exercise.

systematicReviews.title: Examining domains of psychological flexibility and inflexibility as treatment mechanisms in acceptance and commitment therapy: A comprehensive systematic and meta-analytic review
systematicReviews.population: Participants across 67 studies and 77 records with a combined sample of 9123 in ACT mechanism research
systematicReviews.method: Meta-analytic review of psychological flexibility and inflexibility as treatment mechanisms in acceptance and commitment therapy
systematicReviews.finding: Changes in psychological flexibility and inflexibility were examined as mechanisms associated with outcomes in ACT research.
systematicReviews.limitations: This is psychotherapy and mechanism evidence, not validation that a Motazen lesson is ACT or treatment. Samples, active comparisons, measurement choices, and clinical exclusions constrain transfer.

systematicReviews.title: Targeting procrastination using psychological treatments: a systematic review and meta-analysis
systematicReviews.population: Participants in 12 treatment studies with a combined sample of 718
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of psychological treatments targeting procrastination
systematicReviews.finding: The pooled treatment effect was small and heterogeneous; a CBT subgroup appeared larger but contained only three studies.
systematicReviews.limitations: The evidence base was small and heterogeneous and concerned treatment studies. It does not justify promising that a brief productivity technique will resolve persistent procrastination.

systematicReviews.title: Time to Form a Habit: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Health Behaviour Habit Formation and Its Determinants
systematicReviews.population: Participants in 20 experimental health-behavior studies with a combined sample of 2601
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of self-reported habit strength or automaticity
systematicReviews.finding: Habit formation time varied substantially by behavior and person rather than following a universal fixed-day rule.
systematicReviews.limitations: Most included studies had high risk of bias, outcomes were self-reported, and the evidence concerns selected health behaviors rather than every daily-life habit.

systematicReviews.title: The use and impact of self-monitoring on substance use outcomes: A descriptive systematic review
systematicReviews.population: Substance-use participants across 41 studies and 126 analyses
systematicReviews.method: Descriptive systematic review of self-monitoring assessment effects
systematicReviews.finding: Among moderate- or strong-quality analyses, self-monitoring was helpful in 29 percent, had no effect in 63 percent, and was detrimental in 8 percent.
systematicReviews.limitations: The domain is substance use and cannot be generalized numerically to ordinary habit tracking. It is nevertheless direct counterevidence to claims that monitoring is universally beneficial or risk-free.

systematicReviews.title: Do implementation intentions help to eat a healthy diet? A systematic review and meta-analysis of the empirical evidence
systematicReviews.population: Participants in implementation-intention studies focused on dietary behavior
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis
systematicReviews.finding: Effects differed between increasing healthy foods and reducing unhealthy foods, and estimates varied with control and outcome quality.
systematicReviews.limitations: This is older, domain-specific dietary evidence; it cannot establish equal effects for all goals or justify presenting if-then planning as sufficient by itself.

systematicReviews.title: Sleep hygiene education as a treatment of insomnia: a systematic review and meta-analysis
systematicReviews.population: People with poor sleep or insomnia in 15 comparative studies
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis comparing sleep-hygiene education with CBT-I or mindfulness-based therapy
systematicReviews.finding: Sleep-hygiene education was less effective than CBT-I, and only subjective measures showed significant improvement in the review.
systematicReviews.limitations: No included study used sham or no-treatment comparison, and acceptability, adherence, understanding, and cost-effectiveness data were absent. Motazen must not present sleep education as insomnia treatment.

systematicReviews.title: Interventions to improve social connections: a systematic review and meta-analysis
systematicReviews.population: Adults in 58 controlled intervention studies with a mean age of 62 years
systematicReviews.method: Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
systematicReviews.finding: Interventions affected objective social contact and perceived connection differently, with strategy-specific differences across those dimensions.
systematicReviews.limitations: The mean participant age was 62 and intervention families were heterogeneous. Results do not imply that more contact always improves perceived connection or that a single exercise fits all adults.
